Q: Postgres automatically converting date and timestamp fields to timestamptz A:

The conversion happens because there exists no function generate_series(DATE, DATE). As such your columns are converted to types that the function can accept. Postgres has arbitrarily picked TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE over TIMESTAMP [WITHOUT TIME ZONE].

For the later, it's hard to say why without seeing the full schema and query. It's likely one or more columns are not the type you expect, so everything has been promoted to TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE, so that the comparisons can work.

Lastly, there's no reason to use TIMESTAMP over TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE (aka timestamptz). The types have the same storage requirements in PostgreSQL, and you won't get weird edge cases around comparisons and conversions. However, remember that all comparisons happen in the time zone set by the client. So if your client is set to EDT, but another client inserted at timestamp in UTC, then your interpretation over what hour or what date that timestamp represents will differ.

Q: How do I get Windows to "refresh" after manually changing the registry entry for the accessibility text scaling? A:

SetTextScaleFactor() modifies the registry entry then calls an undocumented function to send the notification:

RtlPublishWnfStateData(WNF_EOA_UISETTINGS_CHANGED, 0, 0, 0, 0)

You could call this function directly but it's cleaner to just call the supported API.

Q: How to replace products in sympy expressions? A:

Use .subs(u*v, v*u) instead of .xreplace:

x.subs(u*v, v*u).expand()

.xreplace only matches exact nodes, so it won't catch u*v inside larger products like t*u*v, while .subs will.

Alternatively you can also write a helper to preserve canonical order (e.g. v*u) as well:

def commute_uv(expr):
    return expr.replace(
        lambda e: e.is_Mul and u in e.args and v in e.args,
        lambda e: sy.Mul(*sorted(e.args, key=lambda a: (a != v, a != u)))
    )

commute_uv(x).expand()

That way you also don't have to have to manually substitute u*v everywhere.

Small side note:

This still isn't really true partial commutativity because it's basically just a rewrite rule and not an algebraic assumption system. A cleaner solution would be defining a canonicalization function that walks every noncommutative product and sorts only commuting blocks, e.g. reorder u and v only when adjacent, or within the same product, while preserving the position of t. That would simulate partial commutativity more systematically.
